items: `initTransactions()` fences any prior producer with that id
It bumps the epoch and aborts the old open transaction
Coordinator writes commit/abort markers into every touched partition
Reading transactional output requires opting in
LSO is the Last Stable Offset — the read ceiling
`read_committed` waits for the marker: extra end-to-end latency
`sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, groupMetadata)` joins the commit
The offset commit and the output writes land together
Exactly the mechanism behind `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`
`transaction.timeout.ms` (60s) <= broker max (default 15 min)
Otherwise `initTransactions()` fails at startup
Commit is a two-phase marker write — throughput cost is real
Batch many records per transaction, never commit per record

blocks.title: Fatal versus recoverable
blocks.text: `ProducerFencedException`, `OutOfOrderSequenceException` and authorization errors are fatal: close the producer. `KafkaException` on commit is ambiguous only for retriable causes, and `abortTransaction()` is the safe response to most failures.

items: At-most-once suits high-volume metrics only
At-least-once was the pre-0.11 default, still the pragmatic norm
Exactly-once needs `read_committed` consumers to close the loop
Idempotence covers one partition; transactions cover many
`acks=0`: loss is likely under any failure
`acks=1`: loss on leader failover
`all` + idempotence: loss only on total ISR loss
Exactly-once processing inside Kafka, not delivery outside it
An external DB sink still needs idempotent upserts
Or a dedupe key, or the transactional outbox pattern

blocks.title: The consumer decides too
blocks.text: Commit offsets before processing and you have at-most-once; commit after and you have at-least-once. Producer config alone does not set the semantics.

items: Dedupe on a business key or on (topic, partition, offset)
Store that marker with the write itself
A duplicate only hurts if the effect is not idempotent
'set balance to X' is safe; 'add X' is not

caption.text: Part 3 of KAFKA PRODUCERS. Most Kafka data loss is not a broker problem — it is a `send()` whose return value nobody read. This handbook walks the whole producer path: the two threads behind one call, what each `acks` level really waits for, how `batch.size` and `linger.ms` race each other, and why `enable.idempotence=true` is free correctness. Ten pages of dense notes, config recipes and the invariants worth memorizing.
